title: Master of the rules
hook: the former barber Upali is named foremost in the discipline, and at the council he answers Kassapa's questions until the rules are recited (AN 1; Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
tomorrow: The boy who never heard "no cakes"

segments.voice: Yesterday: Upali, the barber the Sakyan princes let go first. Your line was the barber first. Today the barber becomes the one the whole order turns to.

May a monk eat after noon? Who may sleep under the same roof? What counts as taking what isn't given? In a community of people who had left home, questions like these kept coming, and somebody had to know the answers. In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of outstanding disciples, the Buddha calls Upali foremost among those who know the discipline. The man who once cut the princes' hair now holds the rules. Then the teacher dies, and before anyone recites the discourses, someone has to give the elders the rules. Kassapa, leading the council, turns first to the former barber.
screen: `EVERY DAY, QUESTIONS.` → `UPALI KNOWS THE ANSWERS.` → `WHO WILL RECITE THE RULES?`

segments.voice: First, the title. The Pali word is vinaya, the discipline: the monastic rule, and the training it shapes. Upali is called a vinayadhara, one who holds it. Not a lawyer looking for loopholes; a keeper, the way someone keeps a garden. Second, the council. The Vinaya tells it as a conversation. Kassapa asks the elders for their consent, then asks Upali: where was the first of the gravest rules laid down? At Vesali, Upali says. Concerning whom? Sudinna, the son of Kalanda. On what matter? And Upali answers. Then the next rule, and the next: one question, one answer, the whole assembly listening. Third, what each answer holds. Not a bare command, but a story. In the Vinaya, a rule usually comes with how it was laid down: someone did something, people were troubled, and the Buddha made a rule. The rules are remembered as responses, not commands from nowhere. Fourth, why have rules at all? In another discourse, Upali himself asks the Buddha, and the answer lists ten reasons. Among them: for the well-being of the community, for its comfort, for the ease of those who behave well, to restrain troubles in this life and guard against those to come, and so that the teaching lasts. Several look outward, to other people. A rule kept well is a kindness to the ones you live beside.
screen: `ONE WHO HOLDS THE DISCIPLINE.` · `QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS AT THE COUNCIL.` · `EACH RULE HAS A STORY.` · `TEN REASONS FOR A RULE.` · then, large: `THE RULES REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one rule you already keep: a precept, a promise, a house rule, something you never do at work. Do what Upali's answers do: remember where it came from and why, then whom it protects, maybe you, maybe someone across the table, and hold that person in mind for a few breaths. You don't need a new rule; just let the old one become a little warmer.
Vinaya, the discipline. What Upali, the former barber, held and answered for at the council until it was recited in full. Today's word.
Your line: the rules remembered. The barber who knew every one is why the council could recite them. That's day seven hundred forty-seven.

screen: `DAY 747 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BOY WHO NEVER HEARD "NO CAKES".`

howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries the core monastic rules are recited aloud at the regular observance-day gatherings, and Upali is remembered as the elder who recited the discipline at the first council.

chat.says: Aren't monastic rules just a long list of don'ts?
options: Each rule has a story, and many of its reasons look to caring for others.
Yes: they're commands from nowhere, kept just to prove obedience.
They're mostly loopholes that a clever monk learns to work around.
chat.meaning: In the Vinaya a rule usually comes with the story of how it was laid down, and the ten reasons include the community's well-being and comfort.

notes: All paraphrased; Rhys Davids and Oldenberg translated the Cullavagga (SBE 20), but nothing is quoted because the writer was not certain of the exact wording.

Confirm the Cullavagga 11 exchange: where was the first parajika laid down (Vesali), concerning whom (Sudinna, son of Kalanda), on what matter (sexual intercourse, left unnamed here as 'on what matter').
AN 10.31 (Upali): confirm the list of ten reasons and that the five named here are fairly paraphrased. 'Several of the reasons look outward' is the writer's reading of the list; check it.
'In the Vinaya, a rule usually comes with the story of how it was laid down' describes the Suttavibhanga's structure; confirm it is fair as a general statement.
The hook's sample questions (eating after noon, sleeping under one roof, taking what isn't given) are illustrations of subjects the rules cover; confirm.
howItsDone: confirm that the Patimokkha recitation on uposatha days is fairly described.
